forecast.session_note: Pre-event note for 24-28 Aug 2026. The week's USD risk is dominated by July core PCE (26th) and Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote (28th). Critical context for judging any surprise: the dollar's slide to a three-month low (DXY 98.67, RSI14 28.4, below the 99.19 200SMA, at the bottom of the 98.67-101.55 20d range) has been driven by fiscal/institutional concerns - Treasury doubling long-end buybacks to at least $4bn per operation from 9 Sep after the 30y hit a 19-year high near 5.25%, and the yields erasing that relief within 24 hours - not by Fed rate expectations, which are static at roughly one-in-three for a 25bp September hike (Kalshi 32c, funds at 3.50-3.75% after the 9-3 July hold). That means short-dollar positioning is stretched against a theme that data cannot easily confirm, and hawkish surprises land into thinner air than dovish ones. EUR/USD 1.1699 (RSI 74.2, top of range) and GBP/USD 1.3656 (RSI 69.6) sit at the same extreme; USD/JPY 158.7 is testing its 200SMA at 158.22 with a 1SD day of 0.67% and July's coordinated intervention still fresh. Scoreboard on the six prior calls: 2 hit, 1 miss, 3 unclear.

forecasts.event: US core PCE price index m/m, July 2026 (BEA, released with the Q2 second estimate)
forecasts.consensus: 0.2% m/m (previous 0.1%); core y/y expected to ease to about 3.2% from 3.3%

evidence.fact: July PPI (BLS, 13 Aug): final demand ex food, energy and trade services +0.4% m/m after +0.1% in June, led by a 6.5% jump in portfolio management fees - a category PCE takes directly from producer prices, alongside health care.

Post-CPI nowcasts before PPI clustered just at or above the rounding line: Pantheon 0.16% ('it would take a big upside surprise [in PPI] to leave an increase of more than 0.20% looking likely'), Oxford Economics 0.2%, Capital Economics ~0.21%, Goldman 0.23%. Trackers noted estimates were raised after the PPI portfolio-fee spike.

BEA's methodology changes to portfolio management, legal services and software - which independent estimates suggest would shave roughly a tenth off core y/y and damp exactly this pass-through - arrive with the annual update on 30 September, not on 26 August.

July CPI (12 Aug) landed exactly on consensus: headline +0.1% m/m, core +0.2%, core 2.5% y/y, with shelter up only 0.1% and core goods +0.2%. The consumer-side inputs argue for no more than a routine 0.2%.
Recent record of the series: June core PCE printed 0.1% m/m against a 0.2% consensus, i.e. the last observation rounded down, and headline PCE fell 0.1% m/m on the Iran-ceasefire energy drop.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The bridge from CPI plus PPI puts the unrounded estimate in a 0.20-0.27% band, so 0.2% remains the modal print and calling 'above consensus' would over-read a rounding question. What the evidence does establish is that the distribution is skewed: the portfolio-management pass-through is a mechanical, calculable upside input that arrives before the methodology change that would have muted it, so a 0.3% is a live tail while a 0.1% requires the soft-services pattern of June to repeat without help from financial services.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Multiple dated house nowcasts and a hard PPI input point the same way on the level, but all of them straddle the 0.25 rounding boundary, which is what the headline print turns on.
forecasts.whats_priced: Roughly a one-in-three September hike (Kalshi 32c) and a 9-3 hold at 3.50-3.75% already in the record. Sell-side framing since 12-13 August has been that an in-line July PCE is 'good enough' for a hold and that the September decision 'rests on August data', so 0.2% is close to fully discounted. Crucially, the dollar's three-month low was manufactured by Treasury buyback and fiscal-dominance concerns rather than by rate expectations, so a merely in-line print has little in it to reverse the move.
forecasts.asymmetry: Skewed to the upside surprise. A 0.3% would arrive into a DXY that is oversold at the bottom of its 20-day range with EUR/USD RSI at 74.2 at the top of its own - the short-dollar squeeze potential exceeds the room a 0.1% has to extend a move already three weeks old. A soft print largely confirms what is priced and would likely be worth less than 1SD.

reactions.if_outcome: Core PCE 0.3% m/m (or 0.25%+ unrounded with a 3.3% y/y that fails to decelerate)
reactions.then_currency: Likely supports the dollar as September hike odds reprice above one-in-three; EUR/USD would probably be pressured back toward the 1.1627 200SMA, with USD/JPY more likely to hold above its 158.22 200SMA

reactions.if_outcome: Core PCE 0.2% m/m with y/y easing to 3.2%
reactions.then_currency: Limited FX follow-through, sub-1SD moves more likely than not, with the dollar's direction into month-end handed back to Bessent's buyback message and Warsh on Friday
Would likely add to dollar pressure and could see EUR/USD probe above the 1.1699 range high, though the stretched RSI argues the extension may be shallow

forecasts.event: US Q2 2026 GDP, second estimate (BEA), with corporate profits
forecasts.consensus: 1.5% q/q annualised, unrevised from the 30 July advance estimate

evidence.fact: The last two second estimates were both marked down: Q1 2026 was revised down 0.4pp to 1.6% on softer investment and consumer spending, and Q4 2025 down 0.7pp to 0.7% on exports, consumption and inventories.
June wholesale inventories were revised to +0.2% m/m ($944.7bn) from the +0.3% advance reading, with inventories already subtracting 0.7pp from Q2 growth on the advance estimate.

The full June trade report (BEA/Census, 5 Aug) showed the goods and services deficit narrowing $4.4bn to $73.3bn and the real goods deficit down $5.3bn to $94.5bn, with small upward revisions to goods exports - the trade drag that caused the advance miss may be marginally smaller.
The advance detail was internally strong - real final sales +2.2%, consumer spending 3.2%, domestic private final sales 3.9% - so the composition, not the headline, is where any revision shows up.

forecasts.lean_rationale: Consensus is anchored mechanically at 'unrevised', while the two most recent second estimates were both revised down and the one hard new monthly input (June wholesale inventories) came in lower than the advance assumption. That is a weak base-rate signal on small n, offset in part by slightly better final trade data, which is why the lean is held at low confidence.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Second-estimate revisions are close to coin-flips and the evidence pointing lower is two observations plus a one-tenth inventory tweak; nothing here separates decisively from 1.5%.
forecasts.whats_priced: Effectively nothing. The number is stale and shares its 08:30 ET slot with core PCE, which dominates the reaction. Current-quarter momentum has also moved on: the August flash composite PMI printed 56.0, a 52-month high, with services at 56.8, so a Q2 tweak does not change the growth narrative the market is trading.
forecasts.asymmetry: The larger move sits in the combination, not the number. A material downward revision (toward 1.0% or below) landing alongside a soft core PCE would sharpen the 'dual-mandate trap' framing after July's -23K payrolls and could pressure the dollar more than a GDP revision would on its own. An upward revision is likely to be ignored.

reactions.if_outcome: GDP revised down to 1.2% or lower alongside an in-line or soft core PCE
reactions.then_currency: Likely dollar-negative via the growth channel, with EUR/USD more likely to test the top of its 20-day range at 1.1699
Negligible standalone FX impact; the PCE print in the same release would drive the dollar
Mildly supportive for the dollar if it coincides with a firm PCE, but on its own unlikely to be worth a 1SD day in DXY

forecasts.event: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote (symposium 27-29 Aug, theme 'Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy')
forecasts.consensus: No numeric consensus. The benchmark is that a neutral, 'big picture' address is expected - roughly 69% of fund managers surveyed by BofA look for a neutral tone. Read 'above consensus' as hawkish relative to that, 'below consensus' as dovish.

evidence.fact: Warsh described the planned speech at his 29 July press conference as 'like a blank sheet of paper' and has indicated it will not carry a rate-path signal; his tenure since 22 May has cut post-meeting statements to about 130 words, withheld his own dot, and produced deliberately evasive press conferences.

Hawkish institutional backdrop: the July hold drew three dissents for an immediate hike (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan), the July minutes recorded many participants seeing further tightening as likely necessary if inflation fails to moderate, Warsh has used 'there is no soft inflation target', and reporting has him open to voting for a September hike if data warrant.

Offsetting dovish threads he owns personally: the AI-as-disinflation thesis (which about 60% of economists in a Chicago/FT poll dispute), plus a labour market that shed 23,000 jobs in July with 103,000 of downward back revisions.

The Treasury-Fed axis is the live subplot: Treasury's expanded long-end buyback, criticised as suppressing yields that should reflect monetary conditions, gives Warsh an incentive to defend independence and the 2% mandate rather than to signal September.
August jobs (4 Sep) and August CPI (11 Sep) still land before the 15-16 September FOMC, giving him a clean data-dependence excuse to commit to nothing.

forecasts.lean_rationale: His revealed communication strategy - less guidance, shorter statements, no dot - plus two major data points still to come before the meeting makes a non-committal address the most likely outcome, which is exactly what is expected. There is no evidential basis to lean hawkish or dovish on content; the useful work is in the priced-outcome and asymmetry sections.
forecasts.confidence_reason: An unscripted-in-substance keynote from a chair with only two press conferences of track record; markets are still building the vocabulary to translate his phrasing, so even the sign of the reaction is uncertain.
forecasts.whats_priced: Neutral is the priced outcome, not the safe one: roughly 69% of surveyed fund managers expect a neutral tone, September hike odds are pinned near one-in-three, and the dollar already sits at a three-month low on the fiscal/independence theme rather than on rate expectations. Four things are not priced - any reaffirmation or dilution of the 2% commitment, any clarification of how he weights the dual mandate, a public development of the AI-disinflation thesis, and whether he addresses Treasury's buyback at all.
forecasts.asymmetry: Two-sided but not symmetric in mechanism. Given DXY oversold at 98.67 with EUR/USD RSI 74.2, a hawkish read (2% mandate reasserted, independence from Treasury debt management defended) has the cleanest path to a squeeze in a crowded short-dollar trade. A read perceived as dovish or as accommodating Treasury's yield-management agenda would compound the fiscal-dominance narrative that produced the current dollar level - potentially a larger move in long-end yields and gold than in DXY itself. A genuinely neutral address should be a low-volatility outcome, and that is the most likely one.

reactions.if_outcome: Speech read as hawkish - no dilution of the 2% target, explicit willingness to act in September, pointed defence of Fed independence from Treasury
reactions.then_currency: Likely supports the dollar with the sharpest move against the stretched longs; EUR/USD would probably be pressured back toward its 200SMA at 1.1627 and USD/JPY toward the upper half of its 156.68-163.91 range

reactions.if_outcome: Broad philosophical address on payments and frameworks with no September signal
reactions.then_currency: Limited net FX impact; the dollar would likely stay hostage to the buyback story into month-end, with sub-1SD ranges more likely

reactions.if_outcome: Speech read as dovish - AI-disinflation thesis developed, mandate language softened on labour-market grounds, silence on Treasury's intervention
reactions.then_currency: Likely adds to dollar pressure and could see EUR/USD trade through the 1.1699 range high, with USD/JPY more likely to lose the 158.22 200SMA

forecasts.event: BLS preliminary estimate of the 2026 annual benchmark revision to establishment-survey employment (March 2026 level), published with Q1 2026 QCEW
forecasts.consensus: No published consensus; the anchor is last year's record -911K preliminary revision for March 2025. Read 'above consensus' as a materially smaller downward revision than that anchor, 'below consensus' as another very large downward revision.

evidence.fact: Pantheon Macroeconomics (Tombs, Allen) published ahead of the release that the benchmark is likely to show job gains overstated by roughly 200,000 on nonresponse bias - an order of magnitude smaller than the -911K precedent.

BLS modified the ARIMA component of the national birth-death model effective with the January 2026 estimates to incorporate current sample information; NBER work notes an analogous earlier adjustment reduced the size of the 2025 benchmark revision by about 200,000 jobs.
Absolute benchmark revisions have averaged about 0.2% of total nonfarm employment over the past decade, roughly 300K, versus 0.6% last year.

Persistent negative monthly revisions cut the other way: 27 of 35 revisions in the 36 months to December 2025 were downward, averaging -35K, and 2026 has continued the pattern (April -31K, May -43K, then a combined -103K to May and June with the July report).
BLS is confirmed to release at 10:00 ET on 28 August, the same clock minute as Warsh's expected keynote.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The only dated house estimate on the tape points to roughly -200K, and a documented birth-death model change works in the same direction, so the evidence leans toward a far smaller downward revision than the -911K anchor that has conditioned desks. Persistent negative monthly revisions are the main counterweight, and the historical dispersion around benchmark revisions is wide enough that this cannot be held with strong conviction.
forecasts.confidence_reason: One credible published estimate plus a methodology change align, but benchmark revisions have a wide error distribution and there is no consensus number against which the market can be said to be positioned.
forecasts.whats_priced: Very little in FX. The -911K precedent and the political controversy around BLS data have left desks braced for another large negative number, so a modest revision would be a quiet relief rather than a repricing event. The bigger practical issue is timing: a 10:00 ET release colliding with the Jackson Hole keynote means the number may simply be drowned out.
forecasts.asymmetry: Skewed to the downside tail. A revision materially worse than about -500K would revive the 'labour market much weaker than reported' narrative on top of July's -23K payrolls, likely pressuring the front end and the dollar and cutting September hike odds further. A -200K outcome is close to a non-event and would be crowded out by Warsh.

reactions.then_currency: Likely dollar-negative through lower September hike odds; EUR/USD more likely to hold above 1.1699 and USD/JPY to lose the 158.22 200SMA, though a simultaneous hawkish keynote could neutralise it

reactions.if_outcome: Revision around -100K to -300K, in line with the Pantheon estimate
reactions.then_currency: Modestly supportive for the dollar at the margin by removing a feared downside catalyst, but likely overwhelmed by the keynote in the same minute
Would be a genuine surprise and, combined with any hawkish tone from Warsh, could support the dollar into month-end against stretched EUR and GBP longs

forecasts.event: Treasury Secretary Bessent press conference, Treasury Department, 14:00 ET / 18:00 GMT
forecasts.consensus: No numeric consensus. Billed as the unveiling of new Iran sanctions after Bessent's FT op-ed warning of an 'economic D-Day'; buyback and debt-management questions are near-certain.

evidence.fact: Bessent confirmed on CNBC on 20 August that he would hold a Monday press conference to detail planned Iran measures, and Trump has separately threatened an 'economic D-Day' - so the headline itself is largely telegraphed.

Treasury announced on 19 August it would at least double long-end buybacks to $4bn per operation from 9 September; the 30y had hit a 19-year high, the relief rally was fully erased within 24 hours (30y back above 5.24%), and Bessent said the next day he is ready to go beyond $4bn.
This buyback/fiscal-dominance theme, not rate expectations, is what Reuters and others identify as having driven the dollar to a three-month low against the euro on 20-21 August.

Energy backdrop: Brent closed 94.39 and WTI 87.06 on 21 August, retail gasoline is 4.10/gal - a record for the date - with Hormuz disruption ongoing, so sanctions escalation carries an oil-upside channel.

Iran's president has publicly framed a memorandum of understanding with the US as a victory and oil eased through the first half of August on deal expectations, so the sanctions message could equally arrive alongside de-escalation language.

forecasts.lean_rationale: There is no forecastable quantity here and the two channels pull in opposite directions: more explicit yield management is dollar-negative through the institutional-credibility channel that is already driving price, while harder sanctions and a higher oil price are more typically dollar-supportive versus energy importers. Direction depends on which thread he emphasises.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Unscripted headline event with two offsetting transmission channels and a topic set (sanctions) that is already partly telegraphed.
forecasts.whats_priced: The sanctions announcement is expected and the buyback has already been faded once - yields returned above pre-announcement levels within a day, which is itself the market's verdict. What is not priced is the scale and secondary-sanctions reach of the Iran measures, any commitment to expand buybacks beyond $4bn, and any comment on the dollar or on Fed policy that could sharpen the Treasury-Fed tension ahead of Jackson Hole.
forecasts.asymmetry: The dollar-negative tail looks larger: leaning further into long-end purchases would feed exactly the narrative that took DXY to 98.67, and the market has shown it will test it. Oil-driven risk-off would be more visible in USD/JPY, where the 1SD day is 0.67% and Japan's terms of trade are directly exposed, and in commodity FX, than in DXY.

reactions.if_outcome: He signals buybacks beyond $4bn per operation or otherwise deepens the yield-management stance
reactions.then_currency: Likely keeps the dollar under pressure, with EUR/USD more likely to trade through the 1.1699 range high and gold extending

reactions.if_outcome: Aggressive Iran sanctions including secondary measures, with crude spiking
reactions.then_currency: More likely supports USD/JPY given Japan's energy import exposure, and would tend to support the dollar against European crosses on risk-off, partly offsetting the fiscal theme

reactions.if_outcome: Sanctions detail broadly as trailed, no new buyback commitment, no dollar or Fed commentary
reactions.then_currency: Limited FX impact; the dollar would likely mark time into Tuesday's confidence print and Wednesday's PCE

forecasts.event: Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index, August 2026

evidence.fact: University of Michigan preliminary August sentiment fell about 8% to 51.0 against a 54.5-55.0 consensus, ending two months of improvement, with expectations at 50.6 and year-ahead inflation expectations up to 4.3%.

AAA reported the national average at $4.10/gal on 20 August, up 3 cents on the week and the highest ever for that date, with crude in the $80s-$90s on Strait of Hormuz instability - the single most reliable coincident driver of household sentiment.
July payrolls, published 7 August inside the survey window, showed employers shedding 23,000 jobs against expectations of an 83-85K gain, with 103,000 of downward revisions to prior months.

July's internals were already deteriorating: headline 90.8 missed a 92.4 consensus, the Present Situation index fell 3.6pts to 114.9 (weakest since February 2021) and the jobs plentiful-minus-hard-to-get differential narrowed to +3.1pp.

Hard activity and labour data have been firm: initial claims 206K for the week to 15 August (below the 210K consensus, following July's near-60-year low of 189K), Philly Fed 47.4 in August (a five-year high), and the August flash composite PMI at 56.0, a 52-month high.
The Conference Board series is more labour-market-weighted and historically far less gasoline- and headline-sensitive than the Michigan survey, so it does not mechanically follow an 8% Michigan drop.

forecasts.lean_rationale: Four independent inputs inside the reference period - a sharp Michigan miss, record-for-date pump prices, a negative payroll print with large back revisions, and an already-weakest-since-2021 Present Situation reading - point the same way, and the series itself undershot in July. The firm claims/PMI/Philly Fed set is the genuine counterweight and is why this is a modest rather than aggressive lean; the Conference Board index has been unusually anchored around 90 and a one-point miss is not tradeable on its own.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Several aligned leading signals within the survey window, but the Michigan-to-Conference Board mapping is loose and the labour-market inputs the index weights most heavily are still resilient.
forecasts.whats_priced: Sentiment surveys have been heavily discounted as a growth signal through 2026 - consumption has kept running well ahead of confidence, with Q2 consumer spending at 3.2%. Consensus at 90.3 already embeds a further slide. The component the desk should watch is the labour differential, treated as a lead for the 4 September payroll report, rather than the headline.
forecasts.asymmetry: Given how weak Michigan was, a print at or above 90.8 would be the genuine surprise and, into an oversold DXY at the bottom of its 20-day range, would likely produce more dollar reaction than an equivalent-sized miss. A soft headline with a stable labour differential is close to a non-event; a soft headline with the differential collapsing toward zero is the combination that matters for September pricing.

reactions.if_outcome: Headline below roughly 88 with the labour differential narrowing further
reactions.then_currency: Likely mild dollar pressure via lower September hike odds, though with EUR/USD RSI at 74.2 and at the 1.1699 range high, follow-through above the range may be limited

reactions.if_outcome: Headline near 90 with a stable labour differential
reactions.then_currency: Minimal FX impact; sub-1SD ranges more likely as the market waits for Wednesday's PCE
Would likely give the dollar a modest lift against stretched EUR and GBP longs, with DXY more likely to attempt a move back toward the 99.19 200SMA

resolutions.actual: Minutes of the 28-29 July meeting released 19 Aug: many participants judged further tightening could become necessary if inflation fails to moderate; the record detailed the three dissents for an immediate hike. September 25bp hike probability afterwards sat at roughly 31-32% (Kalshi 32c), versus the ~25-31% benchmark, and the dollar fell to a three-month low that week.
resolutions.note: The content was widely characterised as hawkish (ING: 'Fed minutes lean hawkish, but we don't expect a hike'), which is directionally consistent with the call, but the benchmark was explicitly pricing-based and pricing barely moved - prediction-market commentary described the minutes as supporting the existing ~31% probability. Since the hawkishness was already discounted and the dollar weakened on the Treasury buyback story instead, the lean cannot honestly be scored a hit.

resolutions.actual: Trump hosted cryptocurrency and finance leaders in the Roosevelt Room, with remarks touching on digital assets, prediction markets, North Korea and interest rates; separately he said the US is not in talks with Iran. No single FX-defining headline emerged from the event itself.
resolutions.note: Lean was 'no clear lean', which resolves unclear by construction. The topic set skewed to crypto and foreign policy rather than the Canada tariff pause anticipated in the note.

resolutions.actual: 47.4 in August versus a 24.1 consensus (Haver cites expectations of 25.0), up from 41.4 in July and a five-year high; the ISM-adjusted index eased to 57.5 from 58.1.
resolutions.note: Large beat on the side the lean called, though the call was held at low confidence and the magnitude was far beyond anything the evidence supported.

resolutions.actual: 206K for the week ending 15 August versus a 210K consensus; prior week revised up to 212K from 209K; continuing claims 1.799mn.
resolutions.note: Printed below consensus as the lean called, consistent with the low-layoff pattern after July's 189K near-60-year low. The 4-week average still rose to 204K.

resolutions.actual: ONS: retail sales volumes fell 0.5% m/m in July 2026, exactly matching the -0.5% consensus; total spend including online fell 0.6% m/m with online sales values down 3.9%, while supermarkets and alcoholic drinks benefited from hot weather.
resolutions.note: Printed exactly on consensus, so the 'above consensus' lean neither hit nor missed. The hot-weather food and drink support the note relied on was present but offset by a sharp online drop.

resolutions.actual: HCOB France flash manufacturing PMI 51.5 in August versus a 50.0-50.1 consensus, up from 49.8 in July and back into expansion; the composite nonetheless fell to 48.8 from 49.4 on service-sector weakness.
resolutions.note: Clear miss - the lean called below consensus and manufacturing beat by about 1.4pts. Notably the composite did weaken, so the underlying French growth concern was right but expressed in the wrong sub-index.
